body_markdown:
Maybe you saw the sale of[that Ford GT](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/2-1-million-gets-you-a-museum-quality-2006-ford-gt-heritage/) recently, or maybe you just love the idea of a well-preserved piece of automotive history. It makes sense that most car people tend to seek out the best examples of a given model, and often that means finding one with limited usage and therefore low miles on the odometer.


Of course, since seeking out low-mileage or otherwise low-use cars has been popular for a very long time, there are plenty of unscrupulous sellers who see the value in an odometer with a nice low number showing. Older odometers are relatively easy to tamper with and to make them display whatever number you would like. However, the rest of the car is not so easy to tamper with and will tell you if what you are looking at is the creampuff you hope it is or just a shined-up project seeking an enthusiastic buyer. Here are eight places to look.


## Steering Wheel Wear


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Of all the unavoidable places to touch in a car, the steering wheel tops the list. Unless you’re, well, not driving, you more or less have to be touching the steering wheel. Smoother hands might wear a wheel less, but often the oils from your skin combine with small scratches to flake off paint or dull just certain sections of the wheel, regardless of the material it is made of. Also look behind at the indicators and their stalks as these also start to age or wear with usage, though a lot slower.


## Carpet


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


While we often wonder what an engine could say if it could talk, we ignore one of the parts of a car that truly can: the carpet. Whether it’s the toll booth stub that says this car was in Illinois that one weekend in 1994, or sticky change, or a few starchy receipts confirming that diet never stuck, the carpet of a car tells no lies. Especially older carpet with a medium pile construction that can essentially “dent” if a person gets in the habit of resting their heal in the exact same spot when driving.


## Seat Bolsters


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Plenty of cars that would be desirable with lower mileage or usage are also cars with heavily bolstered or sporty seats. Regardless of how aggressive the seats may or may not be, the wear and tear that comes from a person getting in and out of the car can add up fast, but it usually aligns decently well with mileage and usage. Bench seats or vintage buckets are no exception but tend to wear a lot slower.


## Hardware on the Engine


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Cars that don’t get driven typically don’t need a lot of maintenance—or that maintenance gets deferred due to the lack of driving. This means that things under the hood should not only be complete but the hardware should appear that it hasn’t been marred by tools.


Look for items like the fragile and easily removed clips that hold things like wires and small hoses together, as it’s not uncommon for a mechanic to have to shift and move bundles during a larger service, which can break these. Look for replacement alternators or other items like water pumps that show less age than the surrounding, harder to change, engine accessories.


## Decals and Paint Markings


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Here you’re looking for a lack of damage or wear on decals and paint markings typically made on parts either before or during the assembly-line process. For modern cars that can be various sizes and shapes of barcodes and QR codes, while on vintage iron it can be seeking out chalk, paint, or grease-pen markings on places like the firewall or under the seats. While these can be duplicated (and in proper restorations they typically are), to do so often requires disassembling the vehicle to get proper access. Also consider exterior decals both in placement and application. Was the factory marking originally under clear coat? Or has there been a little undisclosed paint patch?


## Plastic Parts


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Plastic can be a blessing and a curse, depending on where it is used in the construction of a car. Many times the fragility of plastic is why it gets the ire of enthusiasts. The act of removing panels to perform a repair on a low-mileage original can cause damage, as this photo shows our own[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/) fixing a careless mistake from a previous repair using the[plastic welding](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-to-repair-broken-plastic-trim-in-the-comfort-of-home/) technique.


This is especially true for cars that have common failure points, most of which were replaced with superceeded parts visible to the trained eye. Only the low-mile original would still have the “defective” bits in place, surviving the test of time. Additionally, items like air filter housings or vacuum connections age with heat cycles, and most low-mileage cars rarely spend a ton of time idling with high underhood temperatures, so most of these items should still be in great condition.


## Period-Correct Tires


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


It didn’t get driven, so why would the tires be worn out? Original tires can be common from an individual selling a car, but unfortunately all too often period-correct or even original-equipment tires are pulled by well-meaning dealerships when low-mileage cars come through. While it’s not guaranteed to be an option, checking the age of the tires can give you a good feel for usage. When I purchased my 1985 Corvette in 2024, it wore tires with little wear and date codes from pre-2000. Although the car was still over 100,000 miles, the tires told a usage story of the last two decades, and it was not one of heavy right-foot driving.


Tires can tell stories, and the reproduction Goodyear Eagle VR “Gatorback” tires (right) tell a tale of a low-mileage original that the owner would prefer to remain looking original. At some point, the original Gatorbacks became downright unsafe even for low-speed driving, and curators of vehicles with such low mileage tend to go out of their way to keep them looking like they are still brand new cars.


## The Carfax


Sure, it’s not for every car, but when it applies this can be a nice confirmation of your own condition findings—or raise questions about what may or may not align with records. Sites like Carfax are not infallible, since they rely on the end service or dealer to report, but sometimes even sparse reports can confirm low mileage or that a car never left one geographic region.


And, of course, any and all of these can be faked, covered up, or generally made to be misleading. It’s not that any of the above are hard and fast rules but rather points of reference that help to assemble an accurate understanding of what the car is or could be. If you have other items that you use on your checklist to try and confirm or question the accuracy of a car’s mileage, be sure to leave them in a comment down below.
